blocks.h: Why a Fenwick tree instead of prefix sums?
p: A static 2D prefix-sum table answers a query in O(1) but an update costs O(m·n) because it changes many prefixes. A Fenwick tree balances both at O(log m · log n). With many updates and queries this wins.

bullets: Time: O(log m · log n) per update/query; construction O(m·n·log m·log n).

308.takeaway: Mutable 2D range sum: a 2D Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree) stores partial rectangle sums; updates add a delta along the low-bit path, and a region sum is four prefix queries.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: A bipartite graph (boys on one side, girls on the other)
Which boy currently holds an invitation to girl `g` (−1 = free)
Matching array indexed by the girl
`try_boy(b, seen)` (Kuhn's algorithm, a Depth-First Search, DFS, for augmenting paths)
Try to find a girl for boy `b`: take a free girl, or take a girl whose current boy can be rerouted to another girl
Girls already tried in this attempt; prevents revisiting and infinite loops
Girl is free, or her current boy can move elsewhere
Each success adds one more matched pair

blocks.h: Why can a boy 'steal' a girl?
p: If the girl he wants is taken, the code asks her current boy to try another girl (recursively). If that succeeds, the girl is freed and reassigned. This chain is an augmenting path, and repeating the search for every boy finds a maximum matching.

bullets: Time: O(m · m·n) in the worst case.

1820.takeaway: Maximum accepted invitations: maximum bipartite matching with Kuhn's algorithm — for each boy search for a free girl or reroute the girl's current boy.
